findings.title: Google Calendar stores the safeParse wrapper object as the credential key instead of the parsed tokens
findings.description: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed data. The Google caller assigns that return value to `key` and writes `data: { key }` to `prisma.credential.update`. The stored credential becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, so the next read of `credential.key` will not find `access_token`, `refresh_token`, or `expiry_date` at the top level. The previous code stored the output of `googleCredentialSchema.parse`, which was the parsed object. The other callers (Office365, Salesforce, Zoom) read `.success` and `.data` from the result, so the Google call site is the one that is wrong.

findings.title: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `Response` in sync mode, but callers read token fields from it
findings.description: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, the function returns the `fetch` `Response` from the sync endpoint. The non-sync branch returns whatever `refreshFunction` returns, which is a token object for Google and HubSpot. Callers expect the token object in both cases. Google's `refreshAccessToken` reads `res?.data` and then `token.access_token` and `token.expiry_date`, but a `Response` has no `.data` property. HubSpot types the result as `HubspotToken`, which is also not a `Response`. Because the parameter is `() => any` and the return type is inferred as `any`, TypeScript will not catch this. The sync branch must return the same shape the callers expect, or each caller must branch on the mode.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes `credentialId` where every other call site passes `credential.userId`
findings.description: The new `refreshOAuthTokens` call uses `credentialId` as the `userId` argument. The Google, HubSpot, Lark, Office365, Zoho CRM, Zoom, and Webex call sites all pass `credential.userId`. In sync mode this sends a credential ID to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`, which identifies the wrong user. It also means the `userId` truthiness check in `refreshOAuthTokens` does not reflect whether the credential belongs to a user.

findings.title: Office365 video adapter uses the Microsoft Teams app slug
findings.description: The `refreshOAuthTokens` call passes `"msteams"` as `appSlug`. This file belongs to `office365video`, and the sync endpoint uses `appSlug` to choose which credential to refresh. Refreshes for this app would be sent under the wrong slug.

findings.title: Computed-key schema does not express "any numeric property"
findings.description: The keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed from the `toString()` of a Zod schema object. That produces a fixed string such as `"[object Object]"` or a Zod debug string, not a wildcard. The schema therefore does not validate "any property with a number is the expiry" as the comment says, and the `z.unknown()` entry does not allow other properties. The schema should use `.passthrough()` or `z.record`/`.catchall(...)`, with `expiry` validated explicitly.

findings.title: Missing `refresh_token` is replaced with the literal string `"refresh_token"`
findings.description: When the response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets it to the placeholder `"refresh_token"` and returns it. Callers persist the returned data as the credential key, so the stored refresh token becomes a meaningless string. The next refresh will fail with an unclear error, and the original refresh token is lost. The Salesforce caller works around this by restoring `credentialKey.refresh_token`, but the other callers do not.

findings.title: Salesforce checks `response.statusText !== "OK"` instead of `response.ok`
findings.description: The status check compares the free-text reason phrase, not the status code. HTTP/2 responses commonly have an empty `statusText`, so a successful refresh would throw. Error responses with a reason phrase other than "OK" are also handled inconsistently. `response.ok` (or the numeric status) is the correct check. The following `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` branch is also unreachable, because `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on failure.

findings.title: `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is a string or `undefined`, not a boolean
findings.description: The constant is `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Its type is `string | undefined`, and when both variables are set it holds the encryption key itself. The name and the boolean-style checks (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`) suggest a boolean. Wrapping it in `Boolean(...)` or `!!` would make the contract explicit.

findings.title: `.env.example` gives a key-generation command that does not match the documented key size
findings.description: The comment says `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` "must be 32 bytes for AES256", but the suggested command is `openssl rand -base64 24`, which produces 24 random bytes. The header comment in the same block uses `openssl rand -base64 32`. One of the two is wrong; the 32-byte requirement implies `-base64 32`.

findings.title: The webhook secret comparison is plain `!==` and treats a missing header and an unset secret as equal
findings.description: `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` evaluates to `false` when both sides are `undefined`. The `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` gate currently prevents that case, but the handler does not check that the secret is set. A direct comparison of secrets is also not constant-time. An explicit "secret must be configured" check and a timing-safe comparison would remove both risks.
